title: Enterprise SSO and SCIM
subtitle: Let each customer's own identity provider log people in and remove them, and check every answer it sends you.

c.v: On 12 March 2025, GitHub's security lab published a write-up called "Sign in as anyone". It described critical bugs in ruby-saml, a Ruby library that apps use to accept

The library used two different XML parsers while it checked a signature. An attacker could build a document that the two parsers read differently. One parser found one signature. The other parser found a different one. So the check passed on content that was never really signed.
The attacker needed one valid signature from the target company's

. That could come from an ordinary user's login response. In some cases, it could come from the provider's public metadata. With it, they could forge an assertion for any user and log in as that user.

The researchers found a working instance in GitLab. GitLab released a critical patch on 12 March 2025. That was the same day as the write-up. On a GitLab instance with SAML login, "an attacker with access to a valid signed SAML document from the IdP could

GitLab's stopgaps show where the flaw was. Turn on two-factor login inside GitLab. Require admin approval for new users created on the fly. Multi-factor login at the identity provider "does not mitigate this vulnerability".
The flaw was in the SAML library inside the app. The forged login never passed through the provider, so nothing the provider did could stop it.
The lesson: when a customer's identity provider logs users in to your app, your app must check every answer it receives. One weak check, and anyone can be anyone.

q.v: Your SAML library finds the signature and the assertion with two different lookups. An attacker adds a second, unsigned assertion. What is the risk?

options.v: None. The response still has a valid signature.
The library may check the signed assertion but read the user from the unsigned one.
The IdP will reject the response before it reaches you.

why.v: This is XML signature wrapping. You must read data only from the element the signature covers. OWASP says to reject assertions outside the signed content.

q.v: Two users sign in with SSO. Both IdPs send the email bob@acme.com. How should your app pick the account?

options.v: By email, because it is the same person.
By the tenant's IdP plus the IdP's stable subject ID.
By the display name and the email together.

why.v: OpenID Connect says only iss and sub together are a stable identifier. Email must not be used as a unique ID. Any IdP can send any email.

q.v: An employee leaves Acme. Acme uses JIT provisioning only, with no SCIM. What happens to their account in your app?

options.v: It stays active in your app. They cannot log in through the IdP, but old sessions and API tokens can keep working.
The IdP sends your app a SAML logout for every user.

why.v: JIT creates and updates users at login. It does not deprovision. Without SCIM, nothing tells your app that the person left.

q.v: Microsoft Entra sends PATCH /Users/123 with active set to false. What should your app do?

options.v: Delete the user and all their data.
Ignore it, because the user can no longer log in through the IdP anyway.
Block the user, end their sessions and tokens, and keep returning the user from GET.

why.v: This is a soft delete. Entra expects the user to still come back from queries. Your app decides what inactive means, so make it end all access.

q.v: Why should you verify that a tenant owns a domain before you route its emails to that tenant's IdP?

options.v: So that one tenant cannot claim gmail.com or a rival's domain and capture other people's logins.
Because DNS is faster than a database lookup.
Because SAML does not work without DNS.

why.v: Domain routing decides which IdP a user trusts. An unverified claim would let any tenant send other companies' users to an IdP it controls.
